questions.q: Why can't Q# simply be wrapped in a `QSharpBackend(QuantumBackend)` class living in the same process as Qiskit-based backends, the way Lesson 11's two Qiskit backends did?
options: Because Q# doesn't support measurement
Because Q#/QDK uses a fundamentally different toolchain and dependency ecosystem than Qiskit, which Lesson 3 already flagged as needing an isolated environment rather than coexisting in one process
Because abstract base classes only work with one SDK at a time
Because Q# circuits cannot return counts
questions.explain: Unlike two Qiskit-based backends (both ordinary Python objects sharing Qiskit's dependency tree), Q# runs through a separate .NET/QDK-based toolchain with its own release cadence -- exactly the environment-isolation concern raised in Lesson 3.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the `NeutralResult` dataclass in the SDK-adapter pattern?
options: To store only Qiskit-specific result formats
To represent a measurement result in an SDK-neutral format (counts, shots, sdk_name, sdk_version) so results from different SDKs can be compared directly
To replace the need for any statistical testing
To automatically convert Q# code into Qiskit code
questions.explain: NeutralResult gives both QiskitAdapter and QSharpAdapter a common return shape, which is what makes cross-SDK comparison (reusing Lesson 7's statistical-testing reasoning) possible without SDK-specific branching in the comparison code.

questions.q: Why does `QSharpAdapter` communicate via `subprocess.run()` rather than a direct Python import?
options: Subprocess calls are always faster than imports
It keeps Q#'s dependency tree in a separate, isolated environment (qsharp-env/) rather than requiring the main process to reconcile Qiskit's and Q#'s packages together
subprocess.run() is required by the Q# license
Direct imports are deprecated in all Python versions
questions.explain: The subprocess boundary deliberately avoids mixing Q#'s and Qiskit's dependency trees in one process, implementing the environment isolation recommended in Lesson 3 for SDKs that aren't designed to coexist.

questions.q: What statistical-testing concept from Lesson 7 does cross-SDK result comparison reuse, according to the lesson?
options: Comparing two observed count distributions against each other for statistical consistency, the same chi-square-style reasoning used against a single theoretical expectation
A completely new testing framework specific to multi-SDK code
Construction tests, since cross-SDK comparison never involves execution
Manual visual inspection of histograms only
questions.explain: Comparing two SDKs' results for the same logical circuit is structurally the same statistical reasoning as comparing one sample against a theoretical expectation (Lesson 7) -- just applied to two observed samples instead of one sample and one theory.

questions.q: According to the lesson, when is building the multi-SDK adapter layer NOT worth the added complexity?
options: Whenever a project might conceivably need a second SDK someday, so it should always be built proactively
For a project that only ever targets one SDK -- building it speculatively 'in case Q# is needed later' is discouraged
Only when running on real hardware, never on simulators
The adapter layer is always worth building regardless of actual need
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly warns against speculative abstraction: build the SDK-adapter layer when a second SDK is an actual, current requirement (comparing vendors, validating independent of one SDK's bugs), not preemptively for a hypothetical future need.
